planting.note: Set lab-propagated rhizome divisions shallowly in fall into gritty, humus-rich, neutral-to-alkaline soil in part shade, mimicking the open alpine meadows and scrub of its native Himalayan range.

directions: Tibetan lady's slipper is a low, clump-forming orchid from high-elevation meadows and scrub of western China and the Himalayan foothills, sold today only as laboratory-propagated seedlings from specialty hardy-orchid nurseries since wild plants are slow-growing and should never be collected. A single large, deep wine-purple to pink pouch flower with a flattened, almost disc-like lip opens atop a short stem in mid to late spring, just above a pair of broad pleated leaves. Give it sharply drained, humus-rich soil with a near-neutral to slightly alkaline pH and dappled shade, and avoid summer waterlogging, which this species tolerates poorly compared with lowland Cypripedium. Established clumps are hardy well into cold climates but resent root disturbance, so site them where they can remain undisturbed for years.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in fall into moist, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in part shade, where they can form multi-stemmed clumps over several seasons without being moved.

directions: Henry's lady's slipper is a taller, more vigorous Chinese slipper orchid, sold as lab-propagated plants by a handful of specialty hardy-orchid nurseries rather than collected from its native forest-edge habitat in central and southern China. Each leafy stem carries two to four smaller, greenish-yellow pouch flowers in late spring, opening in succession rather than all at once, which extends the bloom display longer than many of its relatives. It prefers consistently moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled woodland shade and is considered one of the more forgiving Asian Cypripedium for garden culture once established. Leave clumps undisturbed to bulk up, since recovery from transplant shock can take a full growing season or more.

planting.note: Set lab-propagated rhizomes shallowly in fall into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, and protect emerging spring shoots from late frost.

directions: Striped lady's slipper takes its common name from the fine brown streaking on its pale yellow to chartreuse pouch flower, borne singly or in pairs above hairy stems clothed in broad, parallel-veined leaves. It grows wild on forested slopes of Sichuan, Hubei, and Guizhou in China at moderate elevation, but garden stock comes exclusively from laboratory-propagated seedlings offered in limited numbers by a few specialty hardy-orchid growers, since true wild divisions are neither available nor appropriate to plant. It wants evenly moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and part shade, and is somewhat less cold-tolerant than northern Cypripedium species, so a protective winter mulch is worthwhile in the colder part of its range. As with all slipper orchids, avoid moving established plants once they are settled.

common_name: Segawa's Lady's Slipper (Taiwan Yellow Lady's Slipper)

planting.note: Plant lab-propagated divisions in fall into moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade, sited where they will not be disturbed once settled.

directions: Segawa's lady's slipper is a compact Taiwanese species found clinging to steep, forested limestone cliffs, where bright yellow pouch flowers with similarly colored sepals open in spring above a low pair of pleated leaves. Because the species is considered endangered in the wild, every plant offered by the few specialty hardy-orchid nurseries that carry it is laboratory-grown from seed rather than field-collected, and buyers should confirm this provenance before purchase. It has an unusually long growing season for a Cypripedium, with foliage emerging early and persisting later into autumn than most relatives. Grow it in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in dappled shade, and treat it as a species for patient collectors rather than a fast-establishing garden plant.
